title: Project: Inventory Tracker
learningObjectives: Represent product details and quantities with suitable classes
Store products in a Map keyed by unique product identifiers
Update stock safely when receiving or selling product units
Prevent sales that would reduce available stock below zero
Calculate inventory value and report missing product identifiers

understand.concept: Use a product code to find an item. Encapsulate quantity changes so stock cannot become negative. Test adding, receiving, selling and looking up products independently.
understand.whyItMatters: Project: Inventory Tracker helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Model products and identify them reliably

An inventory item needs a stable product code, a description, a unit price and a quantity on hand. A `Product` class or record can represent the product data. A `Map<String, Product>` is useful when the product code is the lookup key: it retrieves an item by code without scanning an entire list. Decide whether product codes are case-sensitive and normalize them consistently if not.

## Keep stock changes inside validated operations

Receiving stock increases quantity; selling stock decreases it. Validate that the requested quantity is positive and does not exceed available quantity before updating the map. Avoid scattering direct `put` and arithmetic operations throughout the application. Put the rules in methods such as `receiveStock(code, quantity)` and `sellStock(code, quantity)`, and report an unknown product code rather than treating a missing entry as zero without explanation.

## Calculate and display inventory value

The value of one product line is unit price multiplied by quantity. Total inventory value is the sum of all line values. Use `BigDecimal` for monetary values when exact decimal arithmetic and rounding rules matter; a `double` example is acceptable for introductory demonstration but should not be used as a financial ledger. Use `LinkedHashMap` when insertion order is useful, or sort entries explicitly when the report needs alphabetical or quantity order.

## Verify important business rules

Test adding a product, receiving units, selling a valid quantity, selling more than available, a zero or negative request, an unknown code, duplicate product codes and a zero-priced item. Verify that failed operations leave stock unchanged. The central invariant is that stored stock never becomes negative.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<String,Integer> stock = new java.util.HashMap<>(); stock.put("PEN", 20); System.out.println(stock.get("PEN")); } }
examples.explanation: Stores each product code as a key and its current quantity as the associated value, allowing the program to retrieve stock by identifier.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { java.util.Map<String,Integer> stock = new java.util.HashMap<>(); stock.put("PEN", 20); int requested = 3; int available = stock.getOrDefault("PEN", 0); if (requested > 0 && requested <= available) stock.put("PEN", available - requested); System.out.println(stock.get("PEN")); } }
examples.explanation: Checks that the requested sale is positive and no greater than available stock before storing the reduced quantity.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int available = 5, requested = 7; System.out.println(requested <= available ? "sale allowed" : "insufficient stock"); } }
examples.explanation: Compares the requested quantity with available stock before accepting the sale, so an order larger than inventory is rejected.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<String,Double> prices = java.util.Map.of("PEN", 2.5, "BOOK", 10.0); System.out.println(prices.get("PEN") * 4 + prices.get("BOOK")); } }
examples.explanation: Multiplies each product price by its quantity to calculate the value represented by the inventory entries.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<String,Integer> stock = new java.util.LinkedHashMap<>(); stock.put("PEN", 20); stock.put("BOOK", 5); System.out.println(stock.keySet()); } }
examples.explanation: Uses LinkedHashMap to retain insertion order when iterating over product codes, making the inventory listing predictable.

practise.guidedTask: Create a Product record and a Map keyed by product code. Implement add, receive-stock, sell-stock and lookup operations with quantity validation.
practise.independentTask: Build an inventory summary that calculates total stock value, lists low-stock items and preserves a predictable display order.
hints: Use the product code as a stable Map key and decide whether code matching is case-sensitive.
Validate positive quantities and available stock before updating; failed sales must leave stock unchanged.
Test unknown codes, duplicate products, zero or negative requests and total inventory value.
practise.challenge: Test unknown product codes, duplicate codes, zero quantity, selling more than available and a product whose price is zero.

questions.prompt: Why is a Map useful for an inventory tracker?
options: It associates a product key with its record or quantity
It guarantees that all values are sorted
questions.answer: It associates a product key with its record or quantity
questions.explanation: A Map associates a product identifier with its product record or quantity, enabling lookup by key rather than scanning every item.

questions.prompt: What should a stock update prevent?
options: A quantity becoming negative when selling unavailable stock
questions.answer: A quantity becoming negative when selling unavailable stock
questions.explanation: A sale must be rejected if it would reduce available stock below zero; failed operations should leave the stored quantity unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which operation is appropriate when receiving more stock?
questions.explanation: Receiving stock adds the accepted quantity to the existing on-hand amount for that product.

questions.prompt: Why use a product code as a key?
options: It provides a stable lookup identifier
It guarantees a unique display name in every system
It stores the price as a method
It avoids checking whether the product exists
questions.answer: It provides a stable lookup identifier
questions.explanation: A stable product code identifies the same item across operations and provides a reliable lookup key.

questions.prompt: Which test is important for a sale operation?
options: Attempt to sell more units than are available
Test with no quantity change only
questions.answer: Attempt to sell more units than are available
questions.explanation: Overselling is a critical boundary case because it must be rejected without corrupting the stock invariant.
